books.title: The Complete Herbal
books.author: Nicholas Culpeper
books.notes: Historical herbal - read as history, not medical advice
books.summary: Nicholas Culpeper published this English herbal in 1653 so ordinary people, not just Latin-reading physicians, could learn about native plants. It lists hundreds of plants with where they grow, when to gather them, and how people of his time used them. Culpeper also linked each herb to a planet, a mix of botany and astrology. Read it as history: many of its claims were never tested, and some plants in it are toxic.

books.title: Notes on Nursing
books.author: Florence Nightingale
books.notes: Home care basics: air, light, cleanliness
books.summary: Florence Nightingale wrote this short guide in 1859 for anyone caring for the sick at home. Her core advice is fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, good food and close observation of the patient. She argues that many problems blamed on illness actually come from poor care. Much of it still lines up with basic modern caregiving, though nursing science has moved far beyond it.

books.title: Letter on Corpulence
books.author: William Banting
books.summary: William Banting, a London undertaker, published this pamphlet in 1863 after losing weight on a diet his surgeon suggested: cutting back bread, sugar, beer and potatoes. It became one of the first popular diet books, and 'banting' turned into slang for dieting. It is an important piece of diet history, not a plan to follow; talk to a doctor before changing how you eat.

books.title: Discourses on the Sober and Temperate Life
books.author: Luigi Cornaro
books.summary: Luigi Cornaro, a Venetian nobleman, wrote these essays in the 1500s after poor health in middle age led him to a strict, moderate diet. He credits moderation, regular habits and a calm mind for his long, active old age. The exact amounts he ate are not recommendations. The lasting idea is moderation and steady routine.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: Marcus Aurelius (George Long trans.)
books.summary: Written around 170-180 AD as the Roman emperor's private notes to himself, Meditations is a core text of Stoic philosophy. Its main ideas: focus on what you can control, notice that your judgments shape how events feel, accept change, and treat others with fairness and kindness. These ideas still shape modern thinking about resilience. Philosophy, not medical advice.

books.title: The Gospel of Relaxation (in Talks to Teachers)
books.author: William James
books.summary: In this 1899 talk, psychologist William James argues that many people live with needless tension and hurry. Drawing on his theory that the body's actions shape feelings, he suggests relaxing the muscles, slowing down and acting calm to help feel calm. It is an early, readable look at the mind-body link. Historical psychology, not treatment.

books.title: Walden
books.author: Henry David Thoreau
books.summary: Henry David Thoreau describes living for two years in a small cabin he built near Walden Pond, Massachusetts (1845-1847). He writes about simple living, spending less, paying close attention to nature and living on purpose. It is a classic of American writing on simplicity and nature connection.

books.title: My First Summer in the Sierra
books.author: John Muir
books.summary: John Muir's journal of the summer of 1869, spent with a sheep flock in California's Sierra Nevada, published in 1911. He records plants, animals, weather and his sheer joy at being in the mountains. It helped inspire the American conservation movement and is a model of slowing down to notice nature.

books.title: The Genuine Works of Hippocrates (Adams trans.)
books.author: Hippocrates
books.notes: Airs, Waters, Places - environment and health
books.summary: Francis Adams's 1849 English translation of writings credited to Hippocrates, the ancient Greek physician. This volume includes 'On Airs, Waters, and Places', which ties health to climate, water, seasons and surroundings, and treats disease as natural rather than supernatural. Many of its medical ideas, such as the four humors, are long outdated. Read it as the history of medicine.

books.title: Self-Help
books.author: Samuel Smiles
books.summary: Samuel Smiles's 1859 bestseller tells short life stories of inventors, artists and workers who succeeded through effort, patience and character. Its message: steady work, self-education and perseverance build a good life. Some views reflect its era, but its focus on habits and persistence still reads well.

tips.tip_trick: Before checking your phone in the morning, take a few slow, deep breaths.
Choose water instead of a sugary drink with your meals.
Spend some time outside every day, ideally in the morning daylight.
Fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables.
Pick a set wake-up time and keep it on weekends too.
Choose whole grains over refined grains. They have more fiber.
Try a gratitude journal: write down one thing you're thankful for today.
Crack a window for a few minutes to bring in fresh air, if it's safe and comfortable to do so.
Take a 10-minute walk today. Some activity is better than none.
Chamomile tea can be a caffeine-free evening drink. Skip it if you're allergic to ragweed or daisies, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you take medications.
Put screens away (or set Do Not Disturb) for the last hour before bed.
Mix up your protein: beans, nuts, eggs, fish and lean meat.
Rinse fruit and vegetables under running water before you peel or cut them.
Get up and move for a minute every hour you sit. Move more, sit less.
Brush twice a day and clean between your teeth once a day.
When stressed, take a few minutes for slow, deep breathing.
Swap one sugary drink a day for water or sparkling water.
Wash your hands for 20 seconds with soap, especially before eating.
Spend time outside in nature with a friend or family member this week.
Ask your doctor which vaccines are recommended for you.
Make a plan with one small goal for tomorrow and the specific step you'll take.
Call or text one friend or family member today just to check in.
Pack a healthy snack from home so the healthy choice is the easy choice.
Keep a battery carbon monoxide detector near every sleeping area. Check the batteries when the clocks change.
Keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet for better sleep.
Try progressive relaxation: tense, then relax, each muscle group from head to toe.
Put healthy foods where you see them first. Make the healthy choice the easy choice.
Track one habit in a notebook or phone app. Keeping a record helps.
If you're struggling, talk to a doctor or counselor. In a crisis, call or text 988.
Once a week, look back at your record: what worked, what got in the way, one small change.
